jocular

/JAH-kyuh-lur/ — accent on first syllable · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Jocular describes someone who is playful and fond of joking around, always ready with a laugh.

His jocular remarks kept the long car ride from feeling boring.

Example

Even during the stressful debate tournament, the team captain's jocular asides kept everyone laughing and loose.

The blend here—the playfulness combined with ready humor—is exactly what jocular names. Because the remarks are meant to entertain and amuse, jocular is more precise than 'light' or 'funny.'

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

droll: Droll means amusing in an odd, dry, deadpan way — the humor sneaks up on you from behind a straight face. Jocular humor is the opposite in delivery: open, cheerful joking that announces itself with a grin. A droll aside is quiet and sly; a jocular one is laughing already.

facetious: Facetious means joking when seriousness is actually expected — treating a weighty question lightly, which can land badly. Jocular carries no such mismatch: it is playful, good-natured joking at ordinary moments when a laugh is welcome. A facetious answer dodges a serious question; jocular banter just keeps things light.

comical: Comical describes whatever makes people laugh — a face, a mishap, a costume — and the effect can be entirely unintended. Jocular describes a person who jokes on purpose: playful, fond of kidding around, always ready with another gag. A slip on the ice is comical; the friend narrating it is jocular.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

solemn: deeply serious, formal, and dignified

grave: weighty and serious, allowing no jokes

Where it sits · how constantly the jokes keep coming

lighthearted → playful → witty → jocular

lighthearted vs. jocular: Lighthearted is the gentlest word on this scale: it means simply carefree and cheerful, while jocular means actively cracking jokes at every opportunity.

playful vs. jocular: Playful is stronger than lighthearted but weaker than jocular — a playful person enjoys fun and games, while a jocular person turns nearly every conversation into a joke.

witty vs. jocular: Witty is close to jocular but a notch below: a witty person makes clever remarks when the moment arises, while a jocular person is constantly, habitually joking around.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — joc (jocus): joke, jest, pastime (Latin)

Suffix — -ular: relating to, inclined to (Latin)

Put it together: Joc- is the Latin word for 'joke' (jocus) and -ular means 'relating to' — so a jocular person is literally 'joke-related': someone playful, always fooling around and ready with a laugh.

Use the root in a new word: joke: The everyday word joke comes from the very same Latin root jocus, so a jocular person is, quite literally, someone full of jokes.

Word Choice

neutral

Jocular is the warmth of joking — reach for it when someone's humor is playful, affectionate, and meant to entertain. For simple humor or jokes, plain words like 'funny' or 'amusing' are simpler.
